personas.name: Climate Pessimist
personas.world_model: The climate is the binding constraint on food. Hotter summers, longer droughts and erratic rain cut yields across the Mediterranean belt faster than farmers can adapt, and markets keep under-pricing that tail. Once a supply shock starts it feeds on itself: stocks are thin, buyers hoard, and prices overshoot. Calm periods are just the gap between shocks.
beliefs: Heat waves and drought cause supply shocks that markets under-price
A rising price trend tends to keep rising while stocks are thin
Southern European yields are on a structural decline
Calm markets are complacent, not safe

personas.name: Efficient-Market Skeptic
personas.world_model: Prices already contain the news. Every story about heat or war is known to thousands of traders the moment it breaks, so the only reliable edge is to fade extremes. Spikes attract supply and destroy demand, slumps do the reverse, and commodity prices revert to their recent average. Narratives are noise dressed as signal.
beliefs: Prices mean-revert after large moves
Headline risks are already priced in
Extreme forecasts lose money on average
Big thresholds are rarely crossed in a few months

personas.name: Geopolitics Hawk
personas.world_model: Food is a weapon. Export bans, blockades, sanctions and conflict near major exporting corridors move prices far more than weather. Governments protect their own consumers first, so any tightness is amplified by beggar-thy-neighbour policy. The distribution of outcomes has a fat right tail, and that tail is political.
beliefs: Export bans and conflict drive the largest price moves
Governments hoard when markets tighten
Volatility clusters: one shock raises the odds of the next
Trade corridors are fragile chokepoints

personas.name: Adaptation Optimist
personas.world_model: Humans adapt. Drip irrigation, drought-tolerant seed, desalination, precision agronomy and new growing regions offset much of the heat. High prices fund the investment that ends them, and farmers respond to prices within a season or two. Doom forecasts have a long record of being wrong.
beliefs: Technology and irrigation offset most heat losses
High prices trigger a supply response within a season
Doom forecasts are systematically too pessimistic
Production moves to new regions as the climate shifts

personas.name: Macro / Dollar
personas.world_model: Commodities are priced in dollars and financed with credit, so the macro cycle dominates. A strong dollar and high real rates push every commodity down together; easing and a weak dollar lift them together. Crop stories are second order: watch the broad trend across the whole complex, not any single field.
beliefs: Rates and the dollar drive commodities as a complex
Broad trends across commodities persist for quarters
Single-crop stories matter less than the macro cycle
Funds amplify macro moves

personas.name: Land-Grab Realist
personas.world_model: Sovereign buyers from water-poor states are locking up farmland and offtake contracts abroad. That removes supply from the open market permanently and leaves price-takers, including European importers, exposed when harvests disappoint. Structural tightening means the base rate of sharp rallies is higher than the past suggests.
beliefs: Sovereign buyers tighten the open-market supply
Structural scarcity raises the base rate of rallies
Importers bear the risk of every bad harvest
Policy will move to restrict foreign farmland purchases

personas.name: Agronomist
personas.world_model: Crops follow calendars. Planting, flowering and harvest windows decide when weather matters, and the same months tend to rhyme from one year to the next. Read the seasonal pattern in the price series, weigh the stage of the crop cycle, and ignore the noise in between.
beliefs: Seasonal patterns repeat year to year
Weather matters most at flowering and harvest
Post-harvest months usually bring seasonal lows
Yield anomalies show up first in the seasonal shape

personas.name: Crowd Follower
personas.world_model: Nobody knows better than the crowd. Follow the consensus, stay close to the base rates, lean slightly with whatever the price did last, and never bet big against the market. Being roughly right with everyone else beats being boldly wrong alone.
beliefs: The consensus is usually close to right
Short-term trends are worth following a little
Avoid extreme probabilities
Size small against the market
